readings.c1s1:
¶
'''unigenital''' (ū-ni-jen′i-tạl), ''a.'' [< LL. ''unigenitus'', only-begotten, < L. ''unus'', one, + ''genitus'', begotten: see ''genital''.] Only-begotten.

'''unigeniture''' (ū-ni-jen′i-tṳ̄r), ''n.'' [< LL. ''unigenitus'', only-begotten (see ''unigenital''), + ''-ure''.] The state of being the only-begotten. ''Bp. Pearson.''

'''Unigenitus''' (ū-ni-jen′i-tus), ''n.'' [NL., so called from the first word (“''Unigenitus'' Dei Filius,” etc.): see ''unigenital''.] A bull promulgated by Pope Clement XI. in 1713, and directed against Jansenism. {{smaller|It commenced with the words “Unigenitus Dei Filius,” and condemned 101 propositions taken from Quesnel’s “Réflexions Morales sur le Nouveau Testament.”}}

'''unigenous''' (ū-nij′e-nus), ''a.'' [< L. ''unigena'', only-begotten, born of one parent or of one family or kind, < ''unus'', one, + ''gignere'', beget. Cf. ''unigenital''.] Of one and the same kind; homogeneous.

'''uniglobular''' (ū-ni-glob′ū-lär), ''a.'' Having or consisting of a single globular part or formation. ''Geol. Jour.'', XLVII. 6.
readings.c1s2:
¶
'''unijugate''' (ū-ni-jö′gāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unijugus'', having one yoke (< ''unus'', one, + ''jugum'', yoke), + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''bot.'', having but a single pair of leaflets: said of a pinnate leaf.

'''unijugous''' (ū-ni-jö′gus), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', same as ''unijugate''.

'''unilabiate''' (ū-ni-lā′bi-āt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''labium'', lip, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having a single lip or lip-like part: said in entomology of orifices with a single fleshy lip on one side, by which they can be closed.

'''unilamellate''' (ū-ni-lam′e-lāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''lamella'' + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having one lamella or layer; unilaminar.

'''unilaminar''' (ū-ni-lam′i-när), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''lamina'', lamina, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Having one lamina; one-layered; single-layered.

'''unilaminate''' (ū-ni-lam′i-nāt), ''a.'' Same as ''unilaminar''.

'''unilateral''' (ū-ni-lat′ẹ-ral), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''latus'' (''later-''), side, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One-sided; of or pertaining to one side only.
{{smaller block|We note that, although ''unilateral'' movements (the more voluntary) are lost, the more automatic (the bilateral) are retained.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXV. 175.}}
Certain hallucinations, as is well known, are ''unilateral'', i. e. are perceived when (say) the right eye or ear is acting, but cease when that action is obstructed, though the left eye or ear is free.
{{right|''Mind'', X. 170.}}
''Unilateral'' lesions. {{right|''Princeton Rev.'', July, 1879, p. 106.}}}}
'''2.''' In ''bot.'', one-sided; either originating on one side of an axis or all turned to one side, as the
readings.c1s4:
¶
{{smaller block|The outer or “sporting” door was of course wide open; passing through an interior one of green baize, I blundered up a narrow and totally ''unilluminated'' passage.
{{right|''C. A. Bristed'', English University, p. 73.}}}}
'''2.''' Ignorant.

'''unillusory''' (un-i-lū′sọ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not producing or causing illusion, deception, fallaciousness, or the like; not illusory; not deceptive. ''Bulwer'', My Novel, iii. 22.

'''unilobar''' (ū-ni-lō′bär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''lobus'', lobe, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''unilobed.''

'''unilobed''' (ū′ni-lōbd), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''lobus'', lobe, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''entom.'', having a single lobe: especially noting the maxillæ of certain insects.
readings.c2s1:
¶
'''unilocular''' (ū-ni-lok′ụ̄-lär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''loculus'', compartment, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''bot.'', ''zoöl.'', and ''pathol.'', having but one loculus, cavity, or compartment; single-chambered; monothalamous, as a foraminifer; uniloculate: as, a ''unilocular'' pericarp or anther; a ''unilocular'' heart or shell: correlated with ''bilocular'', ''trilocular'', ''quadrilocular'', and ''multilocular'' or ''plurilocular''. Also ''monolocular''.

'''uniloculate''' (ū-ni-lok′ụ̄-lāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''loculus'', compartment, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''unilocular''.

'''unimaginable''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bl), ''a.'' Not imaginable; not capable of being imagined, conceived, or thought of; inconceivable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Things to their thought
So ''unimaginable'' as hate in heaven.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 54.}}
<poem>On every side now rose
Rocks which in ''unimaginable'' forms
Lifted their black and barren pinnacles.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Alastor.}}}}

'''unimaginableness''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimaginable; inconceivableness. ''Dr. H. More.''

'''unimaginably''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unimaginable manner; inconceivably. ''Boyle.''

'''unimaginative''' (un-i-maj′i-nā-tiv), ''a.'' Not imaginative; lacking or not characterized by imagination; prosaic.

'''unimaginativeness''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ̄-tiv-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimaginative.
{{smaller block|Tom was in a state of as blank ''unimaginativeness'' con-}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''unimpeachability''' (un-im-pē-cha̤-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unimpeachable, or not open to objection or criticism; blamelessness. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 343.

'''unimpeachable''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bl), ''a.'' Not impeachable; not capable of being impeached, accused, censured, or called in question; free from guilt, stain, or fault; blameless; irreproachable.
{{smaller block|The ''unimpeachable'' integrity and piety of many of the promoters of this petition renders those aspersions as idle as they are unjust.
{{right|''Burke'', Speech on the Acts of Uniformity.}}}}

'''unimpeachableness''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimpeachable. ''Godwin'', Mandeville, iii. 188.

'''unimpeachably''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unimpeachable manner; blamelessly.

'''unimpeached''' (un-im-pēcht′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not impeached; not charged or accused.—'''2.''' Not called in question; not objected to or criticized: as, testimony ''unimpeached.''
{{smaller block|His general character is ''unimpeached'', and there is nothing against his credit.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Goodrich Case, April, 1817.}}}}

'''unimplored''' (un-im-plōrd′), ''a.'' Not implored; not solicited. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 22.

'''unimportance''' (un-im-pôr′ta̤ns), ''n.'' The character of being unimportant; want of importance, consequence, weight, value, or the like.
{{smaller block|By such acts of voluntary delusion does every man endeavour to conceal his own ''unimportance'' from himself.
{{right|''Johnson'', Rambler, No. 146.}}}}
readings.c2s4:
¶
'''unimportant''' (un-im-pôr′tạnt), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not important; not of great moment; of little account.
readings.c3s3:
{{smaller block|Times of fat quietness and ''unincidental'' ease.
{{right|''Wilberforce'', Life, ii. 194.}}}}

¶
'''uninclosed, unenclosed''' (un-in-, un-en-klōzd′), ''a.'' Not inclosed; not shut in or surrounded, as by a fence, wall, etc.
{{smaller block|Waste and ''uninclosed'' lands.
{{right|''Adam Smith'', Wealth of Nations, i. 11.}}}}

'''unincumber''' (un-in-kum′bėr), ''v. t.'' See ''unencumber.''

'''unindifferent''' (un-in-dif′ėr-ẹnt), ''a.'' Not indifferent. ''Hooker.''

'''unindividualized''' (un-in-di-vid̮′ū-a̤l-īzd), ''a.'' Not separated into individuals or component parts: specifically noting certain rocks or parts of rocks, eruptive in origin, which have an undefined base not resolvable into distinct crystalline forms by the microscope.

'''uninervate''' (ū-ni-nėr′vāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''nervus'', nerve, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' In ''zoöl.'', having but one nervure, as an insect’s wing; unicostate.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', one-nerved, as certain leaves.

'''uninerved''' (ū′ni-nėrvd), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''nervus'', nerve, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''uninervate.'' ''Nature'', XLIII. 454.

'''uninflammability''' (un-in-flam-a-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being uninflammable. ''Jour. Franklin Inst.'', CXXV. 42.

'''uninflammable''' (un-in-flam′a-bl), ''a.'' Not inflammable; not capable of being inflamed or set on fire, in a literal or figurative sense. ''Boyle.''

'''unijugate''' (ū-ni-jö′gāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unijugus'', having one yoke (< ''unus'', one, + ''jugum'', yoke), + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] In ''bot.'', having but a single pair of leaflets: said of a pinnate leaf.

'''unijugous''' (ū-ni-jö′gus), ''a.'' In ''bot.'', same as ''unijugate''.

'''unilaminar''' (ū-ni-lam′i-när), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''lamina'', lamina, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Having one lamina; one-layered; single-layered.

'''unilaminate''' (ū-ni-lam′i-nāt), ''a.'' Same as ''unilaminar''.

'''unilateral''' (ū-ni-lat′ẹ-ral), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''latus'' (''later-''), side, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' One-sided; of or pertaining to one side only.
{{smaller block|We note that, although ''unilateral'' movements (the more voluntary) are lost, the more automatic (the bilateral) are retained.
{{right|''Pop. Sci. Mo.'', XXV. 175.}}

{{right|''Mind'', X. 170.}}

'''2.''' In ''bot.'', one-sided; either originating on one side of an axis or all turned to one side, as the flowers of a ''unilateral'' raceme.—'''3.''' Placed on one side only of a surface; unifacial, as a set of polypites.—'''Unilateral bond''' or '''contract''', {{smaller|one which binds one party only.}}—'''Unilateral leaves,''' {{smaller|leaves which lean toward one side of the stem, as in ''Convallaria multiflora''.}}—'''Unilateral raceme,''' {{smaller|a raceme whose flowers grow only on one side of the common peduncle.}}

'''unilaterality''' (ū″ni-lat-e̤-ral′i-ti), ''n.'' [< ''unilateral'' + ''-ity''.] The character or state of being unilateral.
{{smaller block|This ''unilaterality'' is insisted on by Salesbury.
{{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XXII. 387.}}}}

'''unilaterally''' (ū-ni-lat′e̤-ral-i), ''adv.'' In a unilateral manner; one-sidedly.
{{smaller block|The destruction of the occipito-angular region is incomplete, ''unilaterally'' or bilaterally.
{{right|''Lancet'', No. 3485, p. 1291.}}
He recognized thankfully that the government had abandoned the pretension to settle ecclesiastical affairs ''unilaterally''.
{{right|''Contemporary Rev.'', XLX. 282.}}}}

'''uniliteral''' (ū-ni-lit′e̤-ral), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''litera'', ''littera'', letter: see ''literal''.] Consisting of a single letter: as, ''Y'' is the ''uniliteral'' name of some moths.

'''unillumed''' (un-i-lūmd′), ''a.'' Not illumined; not lighted up.
{{smaller block|<poem>And her full eye, now bright, now ''unillumed'',
Spake more than Woman’s thought.</poem>
{{right|''Coleridge'', Destiny of Nations. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''unilluminated''' (un-i-lū′mi-nā-ted), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not illuminated; not lighted; dark.

{{smaller block|The outer or “sporting” door was of course wide open; passing through an interior one of green baize, I blundered up a narrow and totally ''unilluminated'' passage.
{{right|''C. A. Bristed'', English University, p. 73.}}}}
'''2.''' Ignorant.

'''unillusory''' (un-i-lū′sọ̄-ri), ''a.'' Not producing or causing illusion, deception, fallaciousness, or the like; not illusory; not deceptive. ''Bulwer'', My Novel, iii. 22.

'''unilobar''' (ū-ni-lō′bär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''lobus'', lobe, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''unilobed.''

'''unilobed''' (ū′ni-lōbd), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''lobus'', lobe, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''entom.'', having a single lobe: especially noting the maxillæ of certain insects.

'''unilocular''' (ū-ni-lok′ụ̄-lär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''loculus'', compartment, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] In ''bot.'', ''zoöl.'', and ''pathol.'', having but one loculus, cavity, or compartment; single-chambered; monothalamous, as a foraminifer; uniloculate: as, a ''unilocular'' pericarp or anther; a ''unilocular'' heart or shell: correlated with ''bilocular'', ''trilocular'', ''quadrilocular'', and ''multilocular'' or ''plurilocular''. Also ''monolocular''.

'''uniloculate''' (ū-ni-lok′ụ̄-lāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''loculus'', compartment, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''unilocular''.

'''unimaginable''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bl), ''a.'' Not imaginable; not capable of being imagined, conceived, or thought of; inconceivable.
{{smaller block|<poem>Things to their thought
So ''unimaginable'' as hate in heaven.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., vii. 54.}}
<poem>On every side now rose
Rocks which in ''unimaginable'' forms
Lifted their black and barren pinnacles.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Alastor.}}}}

'''unimaginableness''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimaginable; inconceivableness. ''Dr. H. More.''

'''unimaginably''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ-bli), ''adv.'' In an unimaginable manner; inconceivably. ''Boyle.''

'''unimaginative''' (un-i-maj′i-nā-tiv), ''a.'' Not imaginative; lacking or not characterized by imagination; prosaic.

'''unimaginativeness''' (un-i-maj′i-nạ̄-tiv-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimaginative.
{{smaller block|Tom was in a state of as blank ''unimaginativeness'' concerning the cause and tendency of his sufferings as if he had been an innocent shrewmouse imprisoned in the split trunk of an ash tree in order to cure lameness in cattle.
{{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, ii. 1.}}}}

'''unimagined''' (un-i-maj′ind), ''a.'' Not imagined or conceived.
{{smaller block|''Unimagined'' bliss. {{right|''Thomson'', Liberty, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>To a long low coast with beaches and heads
That run through ''unimagined'' mazes.</poem>
{{right|''Lowell'', Appledore.}}}}

'''unimitable†''' (un-im′i-tạ-bl), ''a.'' Inimitable.
{{smaller block|Thou art all ''unimitable.''
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Laws of Candy, i. 2.}}}}

'''unimmortal†''' (un-i-môr′tạl), ''a.'' Not immortal; mortal. ''Milton'', P. L., x. 611.

'''unimodular''' (ū-ni-mod′ū-lär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + NL. ''modulus'', modulus, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Having only one modulus.—'''Unimodular transformation''', {{smaller|in ''alg.'', a transformation whose modulus is equal to unity.}}

'''unimpaired''' (un-im-pãrd′), ''a.'' Not impaired, in any sense.
{{smaller block|My strength is ''unimpaired.'' {{right|''Cowper'', Odyssey, xxi.}}}}

'''unimpassioned''' (un-im-pash′ọnd), ''a.'' Not impassioned; not moved or actuated by passion; uninfluenced by passion; calm; tranquil.
{{smaller block|He [Anselm] was exiled; he returned the same meek, unoffending, ''unimpassioned'' man. {{right|''Milman.''}}}}
{{smaller block|Such small ''unimpassioned'' revenges have an enormous effect in life. {{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, iii. 7.}}}}

'''unimpeachability''' (un-im-pē-cha̤-bil′i̤-ti), ''n.'' The character of being unimpeachable, or not open to objection or criticism; blamelessness. ''Contemporary Rev.'', LIV. 343.

'''unimpeachable''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bl), ''a.'' Not impeachable; not capable of being impeached, accused, censured, or called in question; free from guilt, stain, or fault; blameless; irreproachable.
{{smaller block|The ''unimpeachable'' integrity and piety of many of the promoters of this petition renders those aspersions as idle as they are unjust.
{{right|''Burke'', Speech on the Acts of Uniformity.}}}}

'''unimpeachableness''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bl-nes), ''n.'' The character of being unimpeachable. ''Godwin'', Mandeville, iii. 188.

'''unimpeachably''' (un-im-pē′cha̤-bli), ''adv.'' In an unimpeachable manner; blamelessly.

'''unimpeached''' (un-im-pēcht′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not impeached; not charged or accused.—'''2.''' Not called in question; not objected to or criticized: as, testimony ''unimpeached.''
{{smaller block|His general character is ''unimpeached'', and there is nothing against his credit.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Goodrich Case, April, 1817.}}}}

'''unimplored''' (un-im-plōrd′), ''a.'' Not implored; not solicited. ''Milton'', P. L., ix. 22.

'''unimportance''' (un-im-pôr′ta̤ns), ''n.'' The character of being unimportant; want of importance, consequence, weight, value, or the like.
{{smaller block|By such acts of voluntary delusion does every man endeavour to conceal his own ''unimportance'' from himself.
{{right|''Johnson'', Rambler, No. 146.}}}}

'''unimportant''' (un-im-pôr′tạnt), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not important; not of great moment; of little account.

{{smaller block|Why did he not tell his counsel, and authorize them to tell a story which could not be ''unimportant'', as it was connected with a rebellion which shook the British power in India to its foundation?{{right|''Burke'', Works, XII. 69.}}}}
'''2.''' Not assuming or marked by airs of importance or dignity. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|A free, ''unimportant'', natural, easy manner.{{right|''Pope'', Letter to Swift.}}}}

'''unimporting†''' (un-im-pōr′ting), ''a.'' Not importing; of no importance or consequence; trivial. ''Bp. Hall'', St. Paul’s Combat.

'''unimposed''' (un-im-pōzd′), ''a.'' Not imposed; not laid on or exacted, as a tax, burden, toll, duty, command, service, task, etc.; not enjoined.
{{smaller block|The very act of prayer and thanksgiving with those free and ''unimpos’d'' expressions which from a sincere heart unbidden come into the outward gesture is the greatest decency that can be imagin’d.{{right|''Milton'', Apology for Smectymnuus.}}}}

'''unimposing''' (un-im-pō′zing), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not imposing; not commanding respect.—'''2.''' Not enjoining as obligatory; voluntary. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>Beauteous order reigns,
Manly submission, ''unimposing'' toil.</poem>{{right|''Thomson'', Liberty, v.}}}}

'''unimpressibility''' (un-im-pres-i-bil′i-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being unimpressible.
{{smaller block|''Unimpressibility'', which impedes memory, is a consequence of resistance on the part of tissue to the usual stimuli.{{right|''E. D. Cope'', Origin of the Fittest, p. 381.}}}}

'''unimpressible''' (un-im-pres′i-bl), ''a.'' Not impressible; not sensitive; apathetic. {{smaller block|Clara was honest and quiet; but heavy, mindless, ''unimpressible.''{{right|''Charlotte Brontë'', Jane Eyre, xxvii.}}}}

'''unimprison''' (un-im-priz′n), ''v. t.'' To release from prison; set at liberty. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>The green lizard and the golden snake,
Like ''unimprisoned'' flames, out of their trance awake.</poem>{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xviii.}}}}

'''unimproved''' (un-im-prövd′), ''a.'' '''1.''' Not improved, in any sense; specifically, of land, not tilled; not cultivated; not brought into a condition for use by expenditure of labor.—'''2†.''' Not tested; not proved. ''Shak.'', Hamlet, i. 1. 96.

'''unimpugnable''' (un-im-pū′na̤-bl), ''a.'' Not capable of being impugned; unimpeachable.
{{smaller block|Mrs. Bolton could not combat a position of such ''unimpugnable'' piety in words, but she permitted herself a contemptuous sniff.{{right|''Howells'', Annie Kilburn, xxiii.}}}}

'''unimucronate''' (ū-ni-mū′krọ̄-nāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''mucro(n-)'', point, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] Having only one tip or point.

'''unimuscular''' (ū-ni-mus′kū-lär), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''musculus'', muscle, + ''-ar''<sup>2</sup>.] Having only one adductor muscle, as a bivalve; monomyarian.

'''Unimusculosa''' (ū-ni-mus-kū-lō′sä), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < L. ''unus'', one, + ''musculosus'', musculous: see ''musculous.''] In ''conch.'', unimuscular bivalves; the ''Monomyaria''. ''Reeve.''

'''unincensed''' (un-in-senst′), ''a.'' Not incensed, inflamed, provoked, or irritated.
{{smaller block|Jove! see’st thou ''unincensed'' these deeds of Mars?{{right|''Cowper'', Iliad, v.}}}}

'''unincidental''' (un-in-si-den′ta̤l), ''a.'' Unmarked by any incidents. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Times of fat quietness and ''unincidental'' ease.
{{right|''Wilberforce'', Life, ii. 194.}}}}

'''uninclosed, unenclosed''' (un-in-, un-en-klōzd′), ''a.'' Not inclosed; not shut in or surrounded, as by a fence, wall, etc.
{{smaller block|Waste and ''uninclosed'' lands.
{{right|''Adam Smith'', Wealth of Nations, i. 11.}}}}

'''unincumber''' (un-in-kum′bėr), ''v. t.'' See ''unencumber.''

'''unindifferent''' (un-in-dif′ėr-ẹnt), ''a.'' Not indifferent. ''Hooker.''

'''unindividualized''' (un-in-di-vid̮′ū-a̤l-īzd), ''a.'' Not separated into individuals or component parts: specifically noting certain rocks or parts of rocks, eruptive in origin, which have an undefined base not resolvable into distinct crystalline forms by the microscope.

'''uninervate''' (ū-ni-nėr′vāt), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''nervus'', nerve, + ''-ate''<sup>1</sup>.] '''1.''' In ''zoöl.'', having but one nervure, as an insect’s wing; unicostate.—'''2.''' In ''bot.'', one-nerved, as certain leaves.

'''uninerved''' (ū′ni-nėrvd), ''a.'' [< L. ''unus'', one, + ''nervus'', nerve, + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.] Same as ''uninervate.'' ''Nature'', XLIII. 454.

'''uninflammability''' (un-in-flam-a-bil′ị-ti), ''n.'' The quality or state of being uninflammable. ''Jour. Franklin Inst.'', CXXV. 42.

'''uninflammable''' (un-in-flam′a-bl), ''a.'' Not inflammable; not capable of being inflamed or set on fire, in a literal or figurative sense. ''Boyle.''<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
